title: Choose how the translation conveyor leads
question: All three preserve the current navy/cyan/yellow translation engine. Choose the composition that should govern the polish.

options.label: Dual-Lane Workbench
options.lineage: the existing translation engine, organized as a working language desk
options.thesis: Source language arrives above; clear English or Tagalog leaves below, with the engine visibly doing the routing.
options.viewport: A 40/60 opening: concise offer and quote action on the left, two horizontal language lanes and the translation engine on the right; the conveyor continues into the service scope below.
options.risk: Can feel like software if the human service copy becomes secondary.

options.label: Center-Stage Engine
options.lineage: a disciplined evolution of the page already on screen
options.thesis: The current centered promise and full-width flag conveyor stay intact, but hierarchy, spacing, and the transition into services become deliberate.
options.viewport: Centered headline, proof-aware service copy, yellow quote action, then one clean full-width conveyor with the engine at its center; a three-part benefit rail begins the second fold.
options.risk: Closest to the incumbent, so the lower page must be polished firmly to avoid feeling like only a better hero.

options.label: Conveyor Journey
options.lineage: the existing engine extended into the page's real Portuguese-to-Tagalog case study
options.thesis: The conveyor becomes the page's reading spine: request, clarify, translate, review, and deliver.
options.viewport: Offer copy and CTA sit above a conveyor with five named stations; the real Portuguese podcast-to-Tagalog proof panel enters immediately below without changing the page's facts.
options.risk: The process can overpower the simpler request-a-quote job if every station competes equally.
